Your grade

Me 20% The quality of your submissions through the semester, and how well you kept control of the development

“The second half of the semester”, Canvas announcement, 18 October 2026.

How your classmates score you

Right after each talk, on your phone, everyone else in the room scores the program, not the slides. From 1 (not at all) to 5 (completely):

  1. I understand what it does and who it is for.
  2. It solves a problem worth solving.
  3. I would use it, or I know someone who should.

You can change your taps until you press Done.

The three things the audience judges: “whether they get it, whether it matters, and whether they would use it.” Canvas announcement, 18 October 2026.

When two talks get the same score

Your score for a talk is the average of your three taps, rounded. If it is the same as for an earlier talk that day (say, both 5), the app asks which was better: drag it into place, then Done.

After that, your scores for that talk are final. There is no going back to an earlier talk.

Front Row screens with made-up sample talks.

From scores to your grade

Only the other day’s presenters count for your grade: they are not competing with you. Your demo score is the median of their scores. Same median: the one more of them put higher in their own order comes first.

Your place on your day gives your demo points, in equal steps: first 40 of 40, last 24 of 40.

Last on your day, everything else full: 40 + 24 + 20 = 84% → 4.

On a band edge, I round up. The top 3 is feedback only.

Total Grade
88% and above 5
76–87% 4
64–75% 3
51–63% 2
below 51% 1

Grade bands: course syllabus. Demo points = 40 − 16 × (place − 1) / (talks that day − 1).

How to give a talk

  • Open with a promise: what they will know at the end that they don’t know now. Not a joke.
  • Say your main point more than once. At any moment, part of the room isn’t listening.
  • Don’t read your slides. Your audience can read.
  • Few words on a slide. A short label next to the picture it explains, not your sentences.

Worth an hour: Patrick Winston, How to Speak, MIT, ocw.mit.edu/how_to_speak

Winston, P.: How to Speak. MIT OpenCourseWare, RES.TLL-005, 2018. Mayer, R. E.: Multimedia Learning, Cambridge University Press: redundancy and spatial contiguity principles.

Then a closing slide with your link. It doesn’t count as one of the five.

In your repository, at esst-prog2.github.io/your-repo/slides/. A presentation, not a live run. Keep to five minutes: we have to finish on time.

Weight space programming

New research: a language model writes the inside of another AI

  • It looks inside another AI and says what it was trained to do
  • With no training, it writes a small player that beats one trained the usual way
  • It rewrites 0.016% of a small language model’s inside, and its maths test score goes from 8% to 48%

I tried it: on backgammon

  • In my backgammon program, a small neural network decides the moves
  • The question: can a language model write its inside, with no training?
  • And if it can: does it play better, and does it learn better afterwards?

Programming a street lamp

Teaching a street lamp

The sky’s colour: three weights

Made-up example. Which skies need the lamp: the TV brightness formula (ITU-R BT.601).

Lamps feeding lamps

The same made-up example: three colours, two layers of two, one lamp.

Zoomed out: my backgammon network

The same thing, with over two million weights. Nobody sets them by hand: training nudges them, game after game.

From random numbers. The programmed network adds a layer in front: 196 units, the board’s code, written by the language model. Quote: 3Blue1Brown (2024).

A trained network looks like this

It plays decent backgammon. We see every number, and still can’t read what it knows.

One layer (1,024 × 2,048, every second row and column) of my backgammon network after a million games. Orange: positive, dark: negative.

How does a language model write weights? It writes code

  • It gets the network and its description: which input is which point on the board
  • It writes a program, unit by unit: “this lamp lights up when a lone checker stands six points from the opponent: 17 rolls out of 36 hit it”
  • It works the numbers out from the rules and from backgammon knowledge; it doesn’t learn them
  • It is not allowed to train; a few dozen times it may measure whether the network plays better

From the language model’s code. Left out: the smaller chances 7–12 points away.

Weight space programming: written like code

The pattern is still there after training.

Takehi, Teoh, Zhang, Khattab (MIT CSAIL): “Sparks of Weight-Space Programming”, 2 November 2026. Images: one corner (196 × 200) of the same layer in my network.

Learning: a head start

The programmed network starts where the random one gets only after a long time, and it ends lower: from 41 to 6.0, against the random start’s 303 to 19.

Mistakes: average loss per decision against a strong program, in thousandths of a point. Same network size, a million games each.

It can write into a trained network, too

To us it is noise. The model wrote its own concepts into the units the network uses least, and left the rest alone.

First layer (52 × 260 of 52 × 2,048) of my backgammon network after 300,000 games, before and after the edit by Claude Fable. Same colour scale in all three.

Rewriting: a drop, then it keeps learning

58.6 → rewritten, no training: 24.2 → kept learning: 14.2. Not rewritten: 54.7.

One run, one starting point, no control: not a result yet, only a promise.

It can read, too: what does a unit do?

  • Ten units in a trained network that nobody wrote: training shaped them
  • Three language models each put into words what every one of them signals
  • They got to the same place: “I’m ahead in the race”, “the opponent got home, I won’t win double any more”
  • Their explanation predicts what the unit does on other positions too

One experiment on my backgammon network, 22 November 2026: Fable, Opus and Astra, then a debate between them.

Who wrote what in my network

A fit can compute it, but not name it

  • If you know the input, you can compute when a unit switches on: a simple fit tells you
  • A small network fitted to it is even more accurate (R² 0.98, the language models 0.94), but it doesn’t say what it means
  • What’s new: the language model puts the computation into words and ties it to the game’s known concepts
  • And it builds a counterexample: where the explanation fails, we don’t understand it yet

Play it

arpadtamasi.github.io/backgammon

The network on this page is the programmed one. It went live on Friday.

What it is good for

  • Write in what we know. It starts ahead, and needs less data.
  • Fix it without retraining. Like a patch, not a rebuild.
  • Read what it learned. And check it, with counterexamples.
  • Teach people back. In my app, the coach explains your moves with the network’s own concepts.

Early, on small networks, in one game. And the same power can hide things in a network.
